title: Physics of Language Models: Part 3.3, Knowledge Capacity Scaling Laws
authors: Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li

findings.claim: Language models store at most about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, and int8 quantization keeps it.

quantities.condition: synthetic factual (biography) knowledge with sufficient exposures; GPT-2/LLaMA/Mistral-style models

findings.bears_on: Central capacity anchor: a knowledge-saturated model carries ~2 bits per parameter of extractable content.

findings.claim: Int4 quantization of a capacity-saturated model cuts its knowledge to 0.7 bits per parameter, while int8 loses nothing.
findings.quote: Quantizing to int8 does not compromise model capacity (even for models on the boundary of 2bit/param); however, quantizing to int4 reduces capacity to 0.7bit/param.

quantities.condition: after int4 quantization of a model at 2 bits/param
after int8 quantization

findings.bears_on: A saturated model needs more than 4 bits per weight to keep its 2 bits/param of knowledge, so b_w.pretrained rises as models saturate.

findings.claim: MoE models with 32 experts lose only 1.3x capacity per total parameter.

quantities.condition: derived: 2 bits / 1.3 for an MoE with 32 experts

findings.bears_on: MoE weights hold somewhat less information per parameter, consistent with experts tolerating lower rates.

findings.claim: Mixing in junk data cuts the capacity for useful knowledge by up to 20x.

quantities.condition: useful:junk token ratio 1:7, useful knowledge seen 100 times

findings.bears_on: Models trained on web data may hold far less than 2 bits/param of useful knowledge, but the weights still encode the junk, so the total content per weight need not be lower.

findings.claim: Language models store at most about 2 bits of factual knowledge per parameter, even in int8, so a 7B model holds ~14B bits.

For the hyperparameter α in this method, a smaller α implies a stronger compensation, but at an increased computational cost. title: Scaling Law for Quantization-Aware Training
authors: Mengzhao Chen, Chaoyi Zhang, Jing Liu, Yutao Zeng, Zeyue Xue, Zhiheng Liu, et al.

findings.claim: Across 268 W4A4 QAT runs (74M-594M parameters, up to 100B tokens), quantization error falls with model size and rises with training tokens and coarser granularity.
findings.quote: Through 268 QAT experiments, we show that quantization error decreases as model size increases, but rises with more training tokens and coarser quantization granularity.
findings.bears_on: The penalty of low-bit weight matmuls shrinks with parameters but grows with tokens per parameter, so heavily trained small models are the hardest case.

findings.claim: Weight quantization error grows faster with tokens than activation error and eventually exceeds it.
findings.quote: Additionally, with more training data, weight quantization error eventually exceeds activation quantization error, suggesting that reducing weight quantization error is also important in such scenarios.
findings.bears_on: At high tokens per parameter b_w, not b_a, becomes the binding precision in low-bit training.

findings.claim: W4A4 quantization-aware pretraining follows a Chinchilla law plus an additive penalty delta = k * D^gD * log2(G)^gG / N^gN, which grows with tokens D and group size G and shrinks with parameters N; fitted W4A4 constants k = 0.1582, gN = 0.2186, gD = 0.0745, gG = 0.7779 (N, D raw counts).
findings.quote: where k, γN , γD and γG > 0 are fitted parameters. We incorporate a logarithmic term for G, as G = 1 (no quantization) yields δp = 0. The magnitudes of γN , γD and γG reflect the sensitivity of the quantization error δp to N , D and G, respectively. The formula indicates that δp increases with D and G but decreases with N .

title: Compute-Optimal Quantization-Aware Training
authors: Aleksandr Dremov, David Grangier, Angelos Katharopoulos, Awni Hannun

findings.claim: With full-precision training followed by QAT, the compute-optimal QAT share of training grows with the total compute budget (86M-2.2B models).
findings.quote: we demonstrate that the optimal fraction of QAT compared to the total training length increases with the total compute budget.
findings.bears_on: The cheapest way to reach a low-bit model reads full-precision weights for part of training; that part shrinks as compute grows.

findings.claim: Chen et al.'s additive QAT penalty grows without bound in tokens, so it predicts infinite loss as D -> infinity; a weight-QAT law that stays bounded is fitted instead (86M-2.2B, 1-6 bits).
findings.quote: the QAT penalty overtakes the Chinchilla loss term at some point with the growth of token count, which causes the limit of the whole expression to approach infinity as Dtotal → ∞.

findings.bears_on: Chen's 1e25 extrapolation (m 0.56 at W4A4) is an artefact-prone upper bound on the penalty growth; additive laws should not be pushed four decades past their fit.

findings.claim: With a full-precision phase followed by weight QAT (ParetoQ quantizers), 4- and 6-bit weights reach nearly full-precision quality at equal total tokens; 1- and 2-bit drop measurably.

title: ZeRO++: Extremely Efficient Collective Communication for Giant Model Training
authors: Guanhua Wang, Heyang Qin, Sam Ade Jacobs, Connor Holmes, Samyam Rajbhandari, Olatunji Ruwase, et al.

findings.claim: ZeRO++ all-gathers block-quantized INT8 weights for the forward pass; with hierarchical partitioning and quantized weights alone, GPT-350M on 30B tokens ends at the baseline loss.
findings.quote: For a more extended case, we also evaluate hierarchical partitioning and quantized weights alone. The results suggest our convergence is identical to the baseline in this case.

quantities.condition: block-based INT8 weight all-gather (qwZ) with hpZ; GPT-350M, 30B tokens; final eval loss 2.121653 vs 2.121762 ZeRO-3 baseline (Table 5)

findings.bears_on: Sharded training already sends weights to the devices that run the matmuls at 8 bits, at no loss.

findings.claim: Without block-wise scaling, INT8 weight quantization diverges at the start of training.
findings.quote: The training with basic (non-blocked) quantization diverged at the beginning so there is no visible data, on the contrary, ZeRO++ is closely aligned with the baseline, and also confirms our previous analysis of better quantization accuracy by using block based quantization.
findings.bears_on: Low-bit weight reads need per-block scales; their overhead belongs in b_w.

findings.claim: Quantizing gradients inside a reduce-scatter hurts accuracy even with block scaling, because summing low-precision values accumulates the error; ZeRO++ sends INT4 blocks and dequantizes before reducing.
findings.quote: The main issue is, even by incorporating block-based quantization to reduce-scatter operation, it will still significantly hurt model training accuracy. The key reason behind is quantization will decrease value precision. And reduction on low-precision values will accumulate and amplify the errors. Therefore, we propose a novel and much more efficient gradient communication paradigm as a general replacement of reduce-scatter collective, where the gradients are compressed using block-based INT4 quantization during the communication to reduce the communication volume, but the full precision is recovered before the reduction operator to preserve training accuracy.

quantities.unit: bits per gradient entry in transport
quantities.condition: block-based INT4 data-parallel gradient reduce-scatter (all-to-all), FP16 restored before each reduction; weights and gradients, not activations

findings.bears_on: The rule that transport can be low-precision but the reduction cannot is the same one TP partial-sum compression follows (MegaScale-MoE, Echo).

findings.claim: INT4 gradient transport (qgZ) raises GPT-350M final loss from 2.1218 to 2.1656; INT8 weight communication alone is lossless; non-blocked quantization diverged.
findings.quote: As shown in Table 5, even with all three optimizations on, the final evaluation loss is only off by 1%.
